newsitem.title: USA: NY precious metals end higher on moderate volumes.
newsitem.headline: NY precious metals end higher on moderate volumes.

text.p: New York precious metals futures ended higher Tuesday, on moderate volumes, with platinum and palladium again the leaders in the complex.

"Sentiment has improved in gold, with good physical demand seen, but producers are now actively pricing forward sales above $350 an ounce and the recovery of the past ten days may yet prove to be another rally in a bear market," Mitsui USA bullion dealer Greg Drury said.
COMEX April gold ended up 90 cents an ounce at $356.10, after seeing a 19-day high at $357.10 intraday. Total estimated gold volume was 32,000 contracts.
COMEX gold open interest rose 224 lots Monday to 183,800 contracts, in data released Tuesday, after falling 16,142 lots in the past week as funds covered larged short positions, traders said.
In the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted $354.00/50, compared to the London Tuesday afternoon fix at $353.10 and the New York close Monday at $353.00/50.

COMEX March silver ended up 2.7 cents at $5.227, but remained within the $5.140-$5.275 range of past week. Meanwhile, May silver which became the active contract Monday, with more open interest, ended up 2.7 cents also at $5.277 an ounce.
COMEX silver open interest fell 6,500 lots to 93,177 contracts Monday, as funds took profits on the recovery in prices from January and as the March/May roll accelerated.

Silver prices could rise as high at $6.00 an ounce by late 1997 as the ongoing deficit between supply and demand draws down silver inventories to critically low levels, New York based industry consultants CPM Group said in their 1997 silver survey published Tuesday.

Since 1989 the amount of silver used by fabricators in the manufacture of jewelry, silverplate, photographic film and paper has exceeded the supply of silver refined from mine production and old scrap resulting in a large drawdown in the above-ground world silver inventories built up in the 1980's.

"The amount of bullion available to the market has declined sharply since the end of 1989 and is estimated to be at the lowest levels in more than 46 years," CPM Group managing director, Jeffrey Christian, said.
CPM Group estimates that at the end of 1996 around 452.8 million ounces of silver existed worldwide in reported and unreported bullion inventories.
"Given our current projections for the silver market in 1997, bullion stocks could fall 36 pct to 289.6 million ounces by the end of 1997, equal to 4.7 months of fabrication demand," the report said.
But platinum and palladium peformed better than gold or silver Tuesday, as concerns about Russian supplies continue to support prices, traders said.
The April NYMEX platinum/COMEX gold spread widened back out to $25.50 an ounce, not far from the contract highs at $26.60 seen on February 13, after a dip below $20.00 last week.
NYMEX April platinum ended up $3.90 an ounce at $381.80, after seeing a fresh 10-week high intraday at $382.00.
NYMEX June palladium closed up $1.90 at $144.35, after seeing a new contract high during the session at $144.50.

Russian exports of platinum group metals are expected to be much lower in 1997 than in 1996 and no palladium will be exported to Japan in March, a spokesman for Russia's platinum group metals export agency, Almaz, said Monday.
--Clive McKeef, New York Commodities Desk, +1-212-859-1641; --email: clive.mckeef @ reuters.com
